analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $10 an hour and the tipped minimum to $5.50, with annual inflation increases.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote, hearing, or floor action before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $10 an hour, 60 days after enactment. It would also raise the minimum cash wage for tipped workers (currently $2.13 an hour) to $5.50, and it would attach both wages to the Consumer Price Index so they rise automatically each year with inflation, rather than waiting for Congress to act again. The Secretary of Labor would have to publish each adjustment in advance. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, especially the roughly millions of tipped workers whose minimum cash wage is currently $2.13 an hour. Indexing to inflation means their wages could no longer fall in real value between congressional wage fights, which historically happen roughly once a decade.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $10.00 an hour, taking effect 60 days after enactment.
Raises the minimum cash wage for tipped employees, currently $2.13 an hour, to $5.50 an hour.
Indexes both wages to the Consumer Price Index, so they increase automatically each year and do not erode with inflation.

Requires the Secretary of Labor to publish each scheduled wage increase in the Federal Register and on the Labor Department website at least 60 days before it takes effect, giving employers and workers advance notice.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers, most directly restaurants (which rely on the $2.13 tipped minimum), fast-food chains, retail, and other businesses that pay at or near the minimum. Those costs would partly be passed to customers through higher prices or absorbed through lower margins, and opponents argued some marginal jobs could be cut or hours reduced.

drawbacks.text: A roughly 38% jump in the wage floor within two months, followed by automatic annual increases, is a large sudden cost increase for small businesses and labor-intensive employers like restaurants that operate on thin margins.
Indexing the wage to inflation means increases continue automatically even during a recession, when opponents argue a higher floor can cost jobs or reduce hours for the workers it is meant to help.
The bill raised tipped workers' minimum cash wage by more than 150%, a change that would restructure pay in the restaurant industry, where servers' wages are currently built around tips.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wage floor has lost most of its purchasing power since 1968, which is the point the bill's title makes, and the increases are the largest proposed in decades, so the burden on employers is real and front-loaded. The automatic inflation adjustment trades a policy benefit (wages never quietly erode again) for a design cost (no flexibility in a downturn). The tipped-wage increase is the most disruptive piece. On balance this is a large, direct transfer to low-wage workers paid for by their employers and, in part, their customers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee and its Workforce Protections Subcommittee until the 112th Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Jesse Jackson Jr. of Illinois introduced the bill on June 6, 2012, with 17 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day it was introduced.
On September 26, 2012, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, its last recorded action.
The bill had 23 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum or tipped wages, especially restaurant and fast-food operators, kept the $7.25 wage floor and the $2.13 tipped minimum unchanged. Workers at or near the minimum gained nothing; the real value of their wages kept eroding.

for.name: Rep. Jesse Jackson Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Catching Up To 1968 Act on June 6, 2012.

for.name: 23 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 23 cosponsors were Democrats and none came from the Republican majority.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee and then in the Workforce Protections Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats and the Republican-led committee took no action on the bill; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would more than double the tipped minimum cash wage from $2.13 to $5.50 an hour, restructuring how restaurant pay is built. Industry groups argue this forces higher prices or lower staffing; servers whose tips already exceed the new floor would be guaranteed a higher cash base.

A $10 floor with automatic inflation increases raises labor costs for large employers of minimum-wage workers. Chains opposed past wage increases on the grounds that higher floors raise prices or cut entry-level hours.
Small employers face the same 38% wage jump on a fast timeline, though many of their workers and customers would also gain from the increase.
